title: Multi-GPU prefetch timeouts and retry strategy deep dive - Zelos Health
summary: Deep technical troubleshooting session on intermittent OOMs & CUDA timeouts during multi-GPU prefetch/peer-copy workloads. Discussed mempool fragmentation, nvlink peer-to-peer prefetch, pinned memory, asynchronous copy semantics, and proposed retry/fallback semantics in the Redwood runtime plus a short plan to run instrumented reproduce tests.
next_steps: Redwood to provide prefetch/allocator debug build and instructions (Connor)
Zelos to run instrumented reproducer with 4xA100 and collect nvprof/cupti traces (Priya)
Schedule a follow-up 1 week after traces collected (Maya)
Share security/compliance note for on-prem kernel modules (Diego)
action_items: Connor Liu: build prefork debug runtime and upload to shared GDrive (due 2026-05-10)
Priya Rao: run 3x reproduce runs with pinned memory enabled and attach traces (due 2026-05-12)
Maya Patel: send summary + pricing note for Dedicated capacity pilot (due 2026-05-07)
transcript:
Meeting started at 14:30 PT. Duration about 52 minutes.

[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros?
[00:10] Priya (Zelos): Hi, Priya here, Head of ML Ops at Zelos. We run a mixed workload for clinical summarization, mostly 8k-context models, multi-GPU. Liam and Evan from infra are here to help.
[00:22] Liam (Zelos): Hey. We see intermittent OOMs and occasional kernel timeouts when prefetching tensors across devices, especially during bursty requests.
[00:30] Connor (Redwood): Thanks. We're going to dig into the runtime behavior — prefetching, mempool, nvlink peer-to-peer, and what triggers these CUDA timeouts. Quick note: transcription may mis-name a few low-level APIs.

[03:12] Connor: Can you describe the pattern you see? Is it steady-state memory growth or sudden jumps?
[03:22] Evan: It's weird, sometimes stable for hours, then at 1–2% of requests we get an OOM on GPU:0 even though aggregate usage reports free memory. The logs show failed cuMemAlloc or cuBLAS launching long kernels, then a CUDA watchdog timeout.
[03:45] Maya: That sounds like fragmentation or pinned memory exhaustion — when prefetch uses page-locked allocations the host-to-device copy queue can saturate. Do you guys use nvlink p2p for inter-GPU copies?
[04:02] Liam: Yes, nvlink enabled, peer-to-peer is allowed. We're doing async peer copies to build a KV-cache shard per GPU then do local inference.
[04:18] Priya: We also have swapping/prefetch that moves KV cache to a cold GPU during low load, then back during spikes. The spikes coincide with OOMs.

[07:30] Connor: Ok. Two likely culprits: (1) mempool fragmentation — small allocations scatter and leave free but unusable holes; (2) too many concurrent outstanding async copies and CUDA streams causing the driver to block and hit the watchdog; or (3) host pinned memory exhaustion causing host->device copy to stall.
[07:50] Evan: How does Redwood's allocator behave? We use the hosted runtime but are evaluating Dedicated.
[08:02] Diego (Redwood SRE): Our default mempool favors sub-allocation for small objects, but when prefetching large KV pages we sometimes switch to direct allocations. We recently changed the evict-on-fragmentation threshold, that may interact with your workload.
[08:20] Priya: Is there an option to prefer bigger contiguous allocations? We suspect fragmentation because the error shows plenty of total free but failed large allocs.

[11:05] Connor: We can force a different allocation path — allocate page-locked staging buffers once per device and reuse them for copies to reduce host pinned churn. Also aggregated async copies using batched p2p may help.
[11:21] Liam: Could nvlink handshake latency explain the timeout? The stack trace references cuStreamSynchronize waiting for a memcpy.
[11:35] Connor: Yes, if a peer GPU's driver is busy with a long compute kernel, the peer copy can block until that kernel yields. On systems with watchdog timers (e.g., single-display GPUs or certain drivers), long synchronous waits can cause kernel timeouts.

[15:00] Priya: The errors sometimes include 'cudaErrorLaunchTimeout' and other times 'out of memory'. We patched our app to backoff but the runtime still crashes.
[15:15] Maya: Let's talk retry semantics. Are your operations idempotent? Prefetches are usually safe to retry but a failed cuBLAS op mid-kernel may leave partial state.
[15:30] Evan: Prefetches are idempotent. We do have stateful ops when merging KV shards, but we checkpoint.

[18:45] Connor: Our recommended approach: (1) make prefetch idempotent and resumable, (2) use a conservative retry with jitter for allocation failures, (3) on repeated failures escalate to fallback: either route to a smaller-model replica or fall back to single-GPU synchronous path.
[19:05] Liam: How do you detect allocation vs transient driver hiccup? Crash logs often show the same error code.
[19:20] Connor: Use two signals: cuMemAlloc failure + system free memory low = allocation issue. If the failure is accompanied by long kernel latencies and driver logs about timeouts, treat as driver stall. We can add heuristics into the runtime.

[22:00] Priya: Can Redwood runtime abort an in-flight request and reschedule onto different GPUs without double-executing model effects? We need strong idempotency guarantees.
[22:15] Diego: We do token-level cancellation, but full-request reschedule requires the model to be stateless or we must snapshot KV cache. For Zelos' workload, we could snapshot per-request offsets and replay tokens on a fallback GPU. It's more expensive but safer.

[25:40] Connor: A tricky bit — prefetch overlap with execution. We often do prefetch+async copies while executing on another stream. If the memcpy's completion is delayed, the execution may stall waiting for the KV slice. If that stall persists it leads to timeouts.
[25:58] Priya: So the overlap is beneficial usually but brittle under burst when many prefetches pile up.
[26:10] Connor: Exactly. One mitigation: limit outstanding prefetches per device, implement circuit-breaker-style backpressure so the scheduler absorbs pressure instead of the driver.

[29:30] Evan: Any low-level kernel flags we can tune? We run on-prem with Ubuntu 22.04, NVIDIA driver 535, CUDA 12.3, and A100s with NVSwitch.
[29:45] Connor: For A100/NVSwitch, peer-to-peer is fast but it still consumes NIC-like buffers. Tuning the number of CUDA streams, max outstanding copies, and the allocator's pinned pool size helps. Also consider increasing the per-process mempool reservation if you have headroom at the host level.

[33:00] Liam: What about CPU pinned memory exhaustion? Are there OS limits?
[33:10] Connor: Yes, the system can run out of mlocked memory. Check ulimit -l and systemd service limits. Also if you have multiple processes doing pinned allocations you'll push the host into swapping. We saw customers hit OOM on the host and then GPU copies fail.

[36:20] Priya: We noted fragmentation timestamps align with heavy deploys when many small models spin up. Could model lifecycle churn cause memory fragmentation in the runtime?
[36:34] Diego: Yes. If you frequently load/unload models and don't consolidate the mempool, suballocations become fragmented. We can trigger a mempool compaction during low traffic windows. That's an option we can add to your Dedicated config.

[39:05] Connor: For retry semantics: immediate retry on transient driver hiccup with a short exponential backoff (max 3 attempts), on repeated cuMemAlloc fail try a bigger fallback: reduce batch size for that request, evict less-used KV pages, or route to Dedicated capacity if available.
[39:30] Priya: Would evicting KV pages during an in-flight request be safe?
[39:40] Connor: Not ideal. Better to block the request until the page arrives or reschedule to a different GPU with the page warm. Eviction mid-execution can corrupt the request state.

[42:00] Evan: We can attach CUPTI traces. What exact events should we capture to correlate timeouts?
[42:12] Connor: Capture memcpy timeline, cuBLAS launches, CUDA driver stalls, and mempool allocation timeline. Use cupti activity (memcpy, kernel) and nvprof-like counters for outstanding copies. Also capture host pinned allocation calls (cudaHostAlloc) if possible. We'll send a script.

[44:30] Maya: On the product side, for Dedicated we'll offer an option that pins a large staging buffer per GPU and uses RU-level backpressure to avoid pinned churn. That requires a config change but should be low-risk.
[44:50] Priya: Sounds good. Two questions: (1) If we move to Dedicated, can Redwood guarantee driver-level configs like enabling peer-to-peer across specific NUMA nodes? (2) For on-prem, do you support kernel modules or do we have to manually manage drivers?
[45:05] Diego: For Dedicated we manage driver config within our SLA. For Private/on-prem we provide a deployment package; customers can choose whether Redwood installs drivers or we provide guidance for validated driver versions. We'll share the compatibility matrix.

[47:30] Liam: Any quick mitigations we can deploy now?
[47:38] Connor: Yes: (1) cap outstanding prefetches per request, (2) enable reuse of a per-GPU staging buffer (reduce cudaHostAlloc churn), (3) increase ulimit for mlock, (4) enable mempool compaction at low-traffic windows, and (5) short retry with eviction fallback to smaller model.

[49:55] Priya: We'll try those mitigations. Priya to run the instrumented runs.
[50:05] Maya: I'll follow up with the debug runtime build and a short doc with configuration knobs. Connor will assemble the trace script. Diego will send the driver/compat matrix.

[51:00] Priya: Thanks, this was helpful.
[51:12] Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll reconvene after traces — schedule a follow-up next week.

[51:30] Meeting ended. Shared artifacts: link to GDrive with initial logs, Redwood doc: /shared/mgpu-prefetch-debug-instructions (internal), trace script (to be uploaded). Some transcript lines may be mis-transcribed due to accents and low audio.
